{"translation_en":"Don’t you think I can stand the sight of blood? Do you think I am so weak—oh, I should like to see your blood, your brains on a chopping block—I should like to see your entire sex swimming in a lake like that—I think I could drink from your skull; I should like to bathe my feet in your rib cage, and I could eat your heart roasted whole!\n\nYou think I am weak; you think that **I love you**, because the fruit of my womb desired your seed; you think I want to carry your spawn beneath my heart and nourish it with my blood—to bear your child and take your name—listen, what is your name? I have never heard your surname—you probably haven’t one, I suppose. I should become Mrs. “Gatehouse”—or Madame Bobacken—you dog who wears my collar, you farmhand who bears my mark on your buttons—I, sharing with my cook, competing with my maid—oh! oh! oh! You think I am a coward and want to run away! No, now I am staying—and let the thunder roll! My father will come home—find his writing desk broken open—his money gone—then he will ring—that bell—two rings for the valet—and then he will send for the sheriff—and then I shall tell everything! Everything! Oh, it will be wonderful to have an end to it—if only it would end—and then he will have a stroke and die!—then we shall all be finished—and then there will be quiet—peace—eternal rest—and the coat of arms will be shattered against the coffin—the count’s line will be extinct, and the valet’s line will continue in a children’s ho—","larger_context_summary":"Julie addresses Jean, her father’s valet, after their sexual encounter during the Midsummer-night crisis at the Count’s estate. They have discussed fleeing together, but their alliance is collapsing under class resentment, fear, and mutual contempt; Jean’s killing of Julie’s canary immediately precedes and helps provoke this violent outburst. Julie imagines Jean mistaking sexual desire for love and expecting marriage, pregnancy, and social advancement. She scorns those possibilities by emphasizing the gulf between aristocratic daughter and servant, while also anticipating her father’s return, discovery of the missing money, official intervention, disgrace, and the possible extinction of the Count’s family line.","interpretive_commentary":"The highlighted words retain a strongly truth-conditional meaning because they represent a definite proposition about Julie’s emotional state: that she loves Jean. Crucially, however, the proposition is embedded under “you think.” Julie attributes it to Jean and immediately repudiates the interpretation, so the occurrence is valuable precisely because it shows that semantic representation need not entail the speaker’s endorsement. Nor is this a performative declaration that creates or confirms a relationship; the surrounding references to marriage, pregnancy, and taking Jean’s name are contemptuously rejected rather than undertaken. The speech is extraordinarily intense, with fantasies of mutilation and repeated cries, but that intensity belongs to the tirade as a whole. The embedded clause itself is a controlled characterization of Jean’s supposed belief, not a reflexive emotional discharge. Deception is likewise not central: Julie may be unstable or contradictory, but here she openly disputes an attributed belief rather than insincerely professing love."}
